title: Updated estimates of somatic growth patterns and sex ratios in albacore (Thunnus alalunga) from the North Pacific Ocean
content:
Abstract

Stock assessments for Albacore (Thunnus alalunga) in the North Pacific Ocean use an integrated, sex-specific model based on the hypothesis that growth and longevity are sexually dimorphic. However, the paucity of sex-specific data available to model somatic growth and understand spatial population structure was a continual source of uncertainty among past studies. We engaged in a geographically expansive sampling effort to obtain recent age, length and sex data from fisheries sources across its North Pacific range and provide an updated growth model and regional estimates of sex ratios more representative of the entire stock of North Pacific albacore. With a more complete sample distribution by sex, a combined sexes model was favoured over a sex-specific model based on both Akaike Information Criterion (AICc) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). The von Bertalanffy growth parameters for combined sexes were L ∞ = 124.4 cm in fork length (L F), K = 0.168 years−1 and t 0 = −2.100 years. Regional (west, central and east Pacific Ocean), fishery-dependent, sample sex ratios ranged from 1.2 to 1.6 males per female for size classes up to 90 cm L F. Individuals 100 cm L F and larger were predominantly males, but large females were collected for all size classes, and males were larger than females in only one age class. In contrast with previous growth studies, our results support the use of a single model to describe growth and longevity of both male and female North Pacific albacore. The convergence of sex-specific growth curves associated with a more complete sample distribution combined with studies from other albacore populations suggests that male-skewed sex ratios among adult North Pacific albacore are likely due to sex-specific migration patterns, habitat preferences, or behaviours that impact their vulnerability to capture.
